lessons.title: Overview of Agricultural Tools and Their Uses
lessons.body: Agricultural tools are the backbone of farming in Africa. From the simple hoe to the ox-drawn plough, each tool has a specific job. In this lesson, you will learn about common tools and their uses. The hoe is the most basic tool, used for digging, weeding, and making ridges. There are two main types: the short-handled hoe for close work and the long-handled hoe for heavier tasks. The machete (panga) is used for clearing bush, harvesting, and cutting. The axe is for felling trees and splitting firewood. The sickle is for harvesting grains like rice and wheat. The plough, often pulled by oxen or donkeys, turns soil to prepare seedbeds. The harrow breaks clods and levels the soil. The planter drops seeds at the right spacing. The wheelbarrow carries heavy loads. In Africa, many farmers still use hand tools because they are affordable and easy to maintain. But knowing the right tool for the job saves time and energy. For example, using a hoe to harvest rice is slow and damages the grain; a sickle is much better. Similarly, a machete is not for digging. You must match the tool to the task. Also, tools are made from different materials: iron for blades, wood for handles. Understanding these basics will help you when you start making or repairing tools. As you go through this module, keep in mind that a well-made tool can last for years if properly cared for. In the next lessons, you will learn safety, maintenance, and how to make your own tools.

lessons.title: Safety Practices in the Tool Making Workshop
lessons.body: Safety is not optional in a tool making workshop. Every year, many accidents happen because people ignore simple rules. In this lesson, you will learn how to protect yourself and others. First, always wear protective gear. Safety glasses or goggles protect your eyes from flying metal chips when grinding or chipping. Leather gloves protect your hands from sharp edges and hot metal. Closed-toe shoes or boots protect your feet from dropped tools or hot sparks. An apron or overalls protect your clothes and skin. Second, keep your workshop clean and organized. A cluttered floor causes trips and falls. Keep tools in their places. Sweep up metal shavings and wood dust regularly. Third, use tools correctly. A wrench is not a hammer. A screwdriver is not a chisel. Using the wrong tool can cause injury and damage the tool. When using power tools like grinders or drills, check the cords for damage. Never use a power tool in wet conditions. Fourth, handle hot metal with tongs or pliers, never with bare hands. Quench hot metal in water or oil safely, away from your body. Fifth, have a first aid kit nearby and know how to use it. For burns, cool with clean water. For cuts, apply pressure and cover. Sixth, work in a well-ventilated area. Fumes from welding, soldering, or painting can be harmful. If you are welding, use a welding helmet and fire-resistant clothing. Seventh, never work alone if you can avoid it. If you must, tell someone where you are and what you are doing. Finally, learn to recognize fatigue. Tired people make mistakes. Take breaks. By following these practices, you can work safely and productively. Remember, a safe workshop is a productive workshop.

lessons.title: Basic Hand Tools and Their Maintenance
lessons.body: Hand tools are the foundation of any workshop. In this lesson, you will learn about common hand tools and how to keep them in good condition. The most important tools for tool making are: hacksaw, files, hammers, chisels, punches, pliers, wrenches, screwdrivers, and measuring tools like rulers and squares. A hacksaw cuts metal. Use a blade with 14 to 18 teeth per inch for general work. Keep the blade tight and replace it when dull. Files shape and smooth metal. Use a single-cut file for sharpening and a double-cut for fast removal. Clean files with a file card to remove metal chips. Store files separately to avoid dulling. Hammers come in different weights. A 2-pound ball-peen hammer is good for general work. Check the handle for cracks and the head for looseness. If the head is loose, replace the handle or wedge it tight. Chisels cut metal. Keep the cutting edge sharp with a file or grinder. Never use a chisel with a mushroomed headâgrind it back to shape. Punches mark or drive pins. Use the right size for the job. Pliers grip, bend, and cut wire. Keep the pivot oiled. Wrenches tighten and loosen nuts and bolts. Use the correct size to avoid rounding the nut. Screwdrivers must match the screw head. A worn tip will slip and damage the screw. Measuring tools like steel rules and try squares must be kept clean and rust-free. For all tools, rust is the enemy. After use, wipe them with an oily rag. Store them in a dry place. If rust appears, remove it with steel wool and oil. Sharp tools are safe tools because they require less force. Dull tools slip and cause accidents. So, sharpen your tools regularly. A few minutes of maintenance each day will save you hours of work and money. In the next lesson, you will learn how to read tool designs.

lessons.title: Reading and Interpreting Tool Designs
lessons.body: Before you make a tool, you need to understand its design. A design is a drawing or plan that shows the shape, size, and parts of a tool. In this lesson, you will learn how to read simple tool designs. Designs can be sketches on paper or technical drawings with dimensions. The most common views are the front view, top view, and side view. These show the tool from different angles. Dimensions are given in millimetres (mm) or inches. For example, a hoe blade might be 200 mm long, 150 mm wide, and 3 mm thick. The handle might be 1200 mm long and 30 mm in diameter. You need to know how to read these numbers. A scale drawing shows the tool smaller or larger than real size. For example, a scale of 1:2 means the drawing is half the real size. You must multiply the drawing measurements by 2 to get the real size. Lines on a drawing have meaning. Solid lines show visible edges. Dashed lines show hidden edges. Centre lines show the middle of round parts. Arrowheads show dimensions. You also need to understand symbols for materials. For example, a pattern of diagonal lines might mean steel. A wavy pattern might mean wood. Sometimes, notes are written on the drawing, like 'weld here' or 'grind smooth'. In Africa, many tool designs are passed down by tradition, but modern designs can improve performance. For instance, a hoe blade can be made from an old car spring, which is tough and wears well. The design must consider the local materials available. You also need to think about the user: a handle should fit the hand comfortably. A blade should be balanced. When you can read a design, you can make a tool that works. You can also modify designs to suit your needs. Practice by copying simple designs and making them. Start with a simple tool like a garden trowel. Measure, draw, and then build. This skill will serve you well.

lessons.title: Selecting Materials for Agricultural Tools
lessons.body: The quality of a tool depends on the materials used. In this lesson, you will learn how to choose the right materials for agricultural tools. The main materials are metals, wood, and sometimes plastic or rubber. For blades and cutting edges, you need steel that can be hardened. High-carbon steel is best because it can be sharpened and holds an edge. Old car springs, files, and leaf springs are good sources of high-carbon steel. Mild steel is softer and not good for cutting edges, but it can be used for handles or brackets. To test if a piece of steel is high-carbon, touch it to a grinding wheel. If it gives off long, yellow sparks, it is high-carbon. If the sparks are short and red, it is mild steel. For handles, you need strong, straight-grained wood that does not split easily. Good choices include hickory, ash, and locally available hardwoods like mahogany or mvule. Avoid softwoods like pine; they break easily. The wood must be dry to prevent shrinking and loosening. You can also use metal or fibreglass handles, but wood is traditional and easy to replace. For fasteners, use bolts, rivets, or welding. Bolts allow you to replace parts. Rivets are permanent. Welding is strong but requires skill. For the connection between blade and handle, a tang that goes into the handle is common. It should be long enough to prevent wobbling. You can also use a socket or a ferrule. When selecting materials, consider the local climate. In wet areas, wood rots quickly, so treat it with oil or paint. In dry areas, wood cracks, so choose a species that resists cracking. Also, consider the cost. Recycled materials are cheap and good for the environment. For example, an old hoe blade can be reforged into a new tool. Always inspect materials for cracks, rust, or defects. A weak material will fail when you need it most. By choosing wisely, you make tools that last. In the next lesson, you will learn how to organize your workshop for efficient work.

lessons.title: Workshop Organization and Workflow
lessons.body: A well-organized workshop saves time and prevents accidents. In this lesson, you will learn how to set up your workshop and plan your work. First, choose a location. It should be dry, well-lit, and have good ventilation. If possible, have a separate area for dirty work like grinding and welding, and a clean area for measuring and assembly. The floor should be concrete or packed earth, not slippery. Second, arrange your tools and materials. Keep frequently used tools on a wall board or in a rack within easy reach. Store materials by type and size. Label shelves or bins. Keep a clear space for assembly. Have a sturdy workbench. A good height is 900 mm from the floor. The bench should have a vice mounted securely. Third, organize your workflow. When making a tool, follow a logical sequence: measure, mark, cut, shape, drill, assemble, and finish. Keep the work area clean as you go. Put tools back after use. This prevents losing them and keeps the area safe. Fourth, manage waste. Have separate containers for metal scraps, wood scraps, and rubbish. Metal scraps can be recycled or used for small parts. Fifth, maintain your equipment. Check power tools before use. Lubricate machines. Replace worn parts. Sixth, plan your day. Write a list of tasks. Prioritize. If you are making many tools, do similar tasks together, like cutting all the blades first, then shaping them. This is called batch production and it saves time. Seventh, think about safety in your layout. Keep fire extinguishers and first aid kits accessible. Ensure good lighting to avoid mistakes. Eighth, keep a small inventory of common materials so you don't run out. By organizing your workshop, you can work faster and safer. A clean, well-ordered workshop is a sign of a professional tool maker. Practice these habits daily.

quiz.q: Which tool is most commonly used for digging and weeding in African smallholder farms?
quiz.explanation: The hoe is the most basic and widely used tool for digging, weeding, and making ridges.

quiz.q: What is the primary use of a machete (panga)?
quiz.explanation: A machete is used for clearing bush, harvesting, and cutting, not for digging or turning soil.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for harvesting rice and wheat?
quiz.explanation: The sickle is designed for harvesting grains like rice and wheat efficiently.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a plough?
quiz.explanation: A plough is pulled by animals or tractors to turn and prepare soil for planting.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why hand tools are still common in Africa?
options: B) They are easy to maintain
C) They are faster than tractors
quiz.explanation: Hand tools are generally slower than tractors, but they are affordable and easy to maintain.

quiz.q: What should you wear to protect your eyes in the workshop?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses or goggles protect eyes from flying metal chips and debris.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep the workshop floor clean?
options: B) To prevent trips and falls
quiz.explanation: A cluttered floor causes trips and falls, so keeping it clean is a safety measure.

quiz.q: What should you use to handle hot metal?
quiz.explanation: Tongs or pliers are designed to handle hot metal safely without burning your hands.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you get a burn?
options: D) Cover with a dirty cloth
quiz.explanation: Cooling a burn with clean water helps reduce pain and prevent further damage.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid working alone in the workshop?
options: B) In case of accident, someone can help
quiz.explanation: Working alone is risky because if an accident happens, no one is there to assist.

quiz.q: Which file is best for fast removal of metal?
quiz.explanation: Double-cut files have two sets of teeth and remove metal faster than single-cut files.

quiz.q: How should you clean a file?
quiz.explanation: A file card is a brush designed to remove metal chips from file teeth without damaging them.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a hammer head is loose?
quiz.explanation: A loose hammer head can fly off and cause injury, so if it wobbles, fix or replace it.

quiz.q: Why should you never use a chisel with a mushroomed head?
options: B) It can shatter and injure
quiz.explanation: A mushroomed head can break off and cause injury; it should be ground back to shape.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store files?
options: A) In a bucket of water
quiz.explanation: Files should be stored separately to prevent them from rubbing against each other and dulling.

quiz.q: What does a scale of 1:2 on a drawing mean?
options: A) Drawing is twice real size
B) Drawing is half real size
quiz.explanation: A scale of 1:2 means the drawing is half the size of the real object, so you multiply by 2.

quiz.q: On a technical drawing, what do dashed lines represent?
quiz.explanation: Dashed lines are used to show edges that are hidden from the current view.

quiz.q: What does a pattern of diagonal lines on a drawing often indicate?
quiz.explanation: Diagonal lines are a common symbol for steel or metal in technical drawings.

quiz.q: Why is it important to consider local materials when designing a tool?
options: A) To make it look traditional
B) To ensure availability and affordability
quiz.explanation: Using local materials ensures the tool can be made and repaired easily and cheaply.

quiz.q: What is a good source of high-carbon steel for tool making?
quiz.explanation: Old car springs are made of high-carbon steel, which can be hardened and holds an edge well.

quiz.q: How can you test if a piece of steel is high-carbon?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
B) Touch it to a grinding wheel and observe sparks
D) Heat it and quench it
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel gives off long, yellow sparks when ground, while mild steel gives short, red sparks.

quiz.q: Which wood is NOT recommended for tool handles?
quiz.explanation: Pine is a softwood that breaks easily and is not suitable for tool handles.

quiz.q: Why should wood for handles be dry?
options: B) To prevent shrinking and loosening
quiz.explanation: Dry wood is stable and won't shrink, which could cause the handle to become loose.

quiz.q: What is a tang in tool making?
options: B) The part of the blade that goes into the handle
quiz.explanation: The tang is the extension of the blade that is inserted into the handle to secure it.

quiz.q: Why is it important to treat wooden handles in wet climates?
quiz.explanation: In wet climates, untreated wood can rot quickly, so oiling or painting helps preserve it.

quiz.q: What is a good height for a workbench?
quiz.explanation: A workbench height of about 900 mm is comfortable for most people to work at.

quiz.q: Why should you keep frequently used tools on a wall board?
options: B) For easy access and organization
C) To save space on the floor
quiz.explanation: A wall board keeps tools within reach, organized, and off the work surface.

quiz.q: What is batch production?
options: A) Making one tool at a time
B) Doing similar tasks together for many tools
C) Making tools in a batch of different types
quiz.explanation: Batch production means grouping similar operations to save time and increase efficiency.

quiz.q: Why is good lighting important in a workshop?
options: A) To make the workshop look nice
B) To avoid mistakes and accidents
quiz.explanation: Good lighting helps you see clearly, reducing errors and preventing accidents.

quiz.q: What should you do with metal scraps?
options: A) Throw them in the rubbish
B) Recycle or use for small parts
quiz.explanation: Metal scraps can be recycled or reused for making small parts, saving money and resources.
